candidates.title: Bone marrow stimulation improves 12-month clinical outcomes after isolated meniscal repair: A double-blind randomized controlled trial.
candidates.authors_short: Pakmanee N, Limitlaohaphan C, et al.
candidates.journal: Knee surgery, sports traumatology, arthroscopy : official journal of the ESSKA
candidates.abstract: PURPOSE: To compare short-term clinical outcomes and meniscal healing on magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) at 12 months between standard arthroscopic meniscal repair and repair augmented with bone marrow stimulation (BMS) in isolated meniscal tears. METHODS: In this prospective, two-centre, double-blind randomized controlled trial, patients aged 18-60 years with an isolated meniscal tear confirmed on MRI were randomized 1:1 to standard repair or repair augmented with BMS. Medial, lateral and bicompartmental tears were included. The primary outcome was the International Knee Documentation Committee (IKDC) subjective score at 12 months. Secondary outcomes were the Western Ontario and McMaster Universities Osteoarthritis Index (WOMAC), Lysholm score, Tegner activity scale, pain on a visual analogue scale (VAS), patient satisfaction, operative time, adverse events and meniscal healing on 12-month MRI (3.0-T) (Crues classification, two-blinded assessors). RESULTS: Fifty patients (mean age 40.2 years; 21 male and 29 female) were randomized; all completed follow-up. Baseline characteristics were balanced; the augmented group received significantly more sutures (4.2 ± 1.4 vs. 3.3 ± 1.1; p = 0.011) and had fewer horizontal tears (44% vs. 76%; p = 0.042). At 6 months, Lysholm and satisfaction scores already favoured the augmented group. At 12 months, it was superior for the IKDC score (82.5 ± 12.6 vs. 56.5 ± 18.5), WOMAC score (14.6 ± 20.0 vs. 41.8 ± 32.5), Lysholm score (91.8 ± 6.4 vs. 72.6 ± 17.2), Tegner activity scale (median 5.0, interquartile range [IQR] 4.0-6.0 vs. 3.0, IQR 2.0-4.0), pain (0.6 ± 0.7 vs. 2.3 ± 2.3) and satisfaction (9.7 ± 0.6 vs. 7.9 ± 1.7); all p < 0.05. MRI healing did not differ between groups (p = 0.783; unhealed: 2/25 [8%] per group); operative time was similar, and no complications occurred within 12 months. CONCLUSIONS: In this cohort, BMS augmentation was associated with superior patient-reported outcomes at 12 months, without additional complications or an increase in operative time. Meniscal healing on MRI did not differ between groups. These positive short-term findings helped to prove the benefit of BMS augmentation, although confirmation in larger trials with longer follow-up and structural assessment is required to clarify the effectiveness, durability and indications of BMS. LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Level I, therapeutic randomized controlled trial.
candidates.score_reasoning: High-quality double-blind RCT demonstrating bone marrow stimulation augmentation improves meniscal repair outcomes with strong clinical relevance, published in a reputable sports surgery journal.
bullets: Adding bone marrow stimulation to meniscal repair produced significantly better pain, function, and activity scores at 12 months compared to repair alone in adults aged 18 to 60 with isolated meniscal tears.
MRI healing rates at 12 months were identical between groups (8% unhealed in each), suggesting the clinical benefit is not explained by improved structural healing on imaging.
The technique added no extra operative time and no complications, making it a low-risk adjunct to consider for isolated meniscal repair pending confirmation in larger, longer trials.

candidates.title: Timing of platelet-rich plasma administration in arthroscopic rotator cuff repair: A systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised controlled trials.
candidates.authors_short: Tareen H, Mostafa OES, et al.
candidates.journal: Knee surgery, sports traumatology, arthroscopy : official journal of the ESSKA
candidates.abstract: PURPOSE: Platelet-rich plasma (PRP) has been widely investigated as a biologic adjunct in arthroscopic rotator cuff repair (ARCR), yet clinical evidence remains heterogeneous. One potential source of variability is the timing of PRP administration, which may influence tendon-to-bone healing. This study aimed to evaluate the effect of PRP augmentation on structural healing and clinical outcomes following ARCR, with particular evaluation of outcomes according to the timing of PRP administration. METHODS: A systematic review was conducted in accordance with PRISMA guidelines and registered on PROSPERO. PubMed, Scopus, Cochrane CENTRAL and Web of Science were searched through 19 February 2026. Randomised controlled trials (RCTs) comparing PRP augmentation with control in adult patients undergoing ARCR were included. Trials were stratified by timing of PRP administration (intraoperative, post-operative-only or combined). The primary outcome was retears assessed by post-operative imaging at ≥6 months. Pooled risk ratios (RRs) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs) were calculated using a random-effects model. Heterogeneity was assessed using I2 statistics. RESULTS: Fifteen RCTs (1214 patients; 647 PRP and 567 control) met inclusion criteria. Overall, PRP administration at ≥6 months was associated with a reduced risk of retears (RR, 0.53; 95% CI, 0.40-0.70; p < 0.001; I2 = 0%). Subgroup analysis demonstrated that intraoperative PRP significantly reduced retear rates at ≥6 months (RR, 0.49; 95% CI, 0.35-0.68; p < 0.001; I2 = 0%) and ≥12 months (RR, 0.52; 95% CI, 0.30-0.91; p = 0.021; I2 = 0%). Post-operative-only PRP did not demonstrate a statistically significant reduction in retears (RR, 0.35; 95% CI, 0.01-8.12; p = 0.54). Absolute risk reduction at ≥6 months was approximately 12%, corresponding to a number needed to treat of 8. Functional outcome scores improved in both PRP and control groups, with significant differences between groups in included studies, but pooled analyses did not demonstrate consistent between-group differences. PRP was not associated with increased complication rates. CONCLUSION: Intraoperative PRP augmentation during ARCR is associated with a statistically significant reduction in retears. The limited post-operative-only PRP protocols do not demonstrate a comparable benefit and preclude a definitive conclusion that efficacy differs according to timing. These findings suggest a potential timing-dependent structural effect of PRP. However, structural improvements did not consistently translate into superior functional outcomes. LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Level I.
candidates.score_reasoning: Well-designed systematic review and meta-analysis of RCTs on PRP timing in rotator cuff repair with direct surgical applicability, clear subgroup analysis, and large pooled sample in a reputable journal.
bullets: Intraoperative PRP during rotator cuff repair reduces retear rates at 6 and 12 months, with a number needed to treat of 8.
PRP given only postoperatively showed no significant reduction in retears, suggesting the timing of application matters for structural healing.
Despite fewer retears with intraoperative PRP, functional outcome scores did not consistently improve compared to controls.

candidates.title: Effect of Excision of the Infrapatellar Fat Pad in Total Knee Arthroplasty: A Double-Blinded Randomized Controlled Trial.
candidates.authors_short: Howard A, Naeem H, et al.
candidates.abstract: BACKGROUND: The infrapatellar (Hoffa's) fat pad is frequently excised during total knee arthroplasty (TKA) to improve exposure, but its role in postoperative pain and function is uncertain. Previous randomized trials and meta-analyses are equivocal, with follow-up limited to 12 months. METHODS: We conducted a single-center, participant- and assessor-blinded, parallel-group randomized controlled trial. A total of 181 patients undergoing elective primary TKA for osteoarthritis were randomized intraoperatively to fat pad excision (removed) or minimal resection (retained). Implants and rehabilitation were standardized. The primary outcome was the Knee injury and Osteoarthritis Outcome Score (KOOS) at 24 months; the secondary outcome was the Oxford Knee Score (OKS) at three, 12, and 24 months. Groups were compared using Mann-Whitney U-tests, and within-group changes over time using Kruskal-Wallis tests. In total, 140 participants were analyzed at 24 months (74 removed, 66 retained; 22% loss to follow-up). RESULTS: Both groups improved significantly across all KOOS subscales and OKS over time (P-values < 0.05), with gains exceeding the minimal clinically important difference on KOOS Pain. There were no significant between-group differences in KOOS or OKS at any time point (P-values > 0.05). The only within-group gain unique to one arm was KOOS Symptoms in the removed group between three and 24 months (P-values < 0.05). The KOOS scores did not improve between 12 and 24 months. CONCLUSION: In this study, excision or preservation of the fat pad did not significantly influence pain or function at two years postoperatively. The absence of change beyond 12 months suggests future trials could shorten follow-up.
candidates.score_reasoning: High-quality double-blind RCT with 181 patients addressing the common intraoperative question of fat pad excision in TKA, providing definitive Level 1 evidence with 24-month follow-up.
bullets: Fat pad excision versus preservation in primary TKA produced no difference in pain or function scores at any point up to two years.
Both groups improved beyond the minimal clinically important difference for pain, meaning the fat pad decision does not appear to affect patient-reported outcomes.
For primary TKA in osteoarthritis patients, surgeons can excise or retain the fat pad based on exposure needs without concern for worse outcomes.

candidates.title: Effect of Prosthesis Selection on Gap Balancing in Robotic-Assisted Cruciate-Retaining and Posterior-Stabilized Total Knee Arthroplasty: A Prospective Randomized Controlled Trial.
candidates.authors_short: Yang C, Zhu K, et al.
candidates.abstract: BACKGROUND: The study aimed to assess the disparities between robotic-assisted cruciate-retaining (CR) and posterior-stabilized (PS) total knee arthroplasty (RA-TKA) regarding flexion-extension gaps, bone resection amount, and postoperative knee function. METHODS: Prospectively randomized into two groups, CR RA-TKA (n = 60) and PS RA-TKA (n = 60), 120 patients were scheduled for RA-TKA. All patients underwent RA-TKA to execute adjusted implant positioning, flexion-extension gaps, bone resection amount, femoral component rotation, and alignment by using a robotic-assisted system, following functional alignment principles, between September 1, 2021, and December 31, 2022. Patients underwent clinical and radiographic evaluations at the 2-year postoperative follow-up. RESULTS: The extension gap results were similar between the two groups; the flexion gap was greater in the PS RA-TKA group, particularly on the lateral side (P = 0.027). Compared with the CR RA-TKA group, the PS RA-TKA group had significantly less bone resection of the lateral posterior condyle (P = 0.048). Although the PS group required less external rotation of the femoral component than the CR group, the difference was not statistically significant (P = 0.225). There were no significant differences in pre- or postoperative clinical scores between the two groups (P > 0.05). CONCLUSION: The CR design demonstrated superior balance in terms of the flexion-extension gap numerical value compared to the PS design. While the PS RA-TKA group required less posterior femoral bone resection and less external rotation of the femoral component, no significant differences in clinical outcomes were observed between the groups at a minimum of two years postoperatively. For most patients who had varus deformity and an intact posterior cruciate ligament (PCL), the CR implant design remains a reliable option. However, for those who have major flexion gap imbalance or PCL deficiency, the PS design is recommended.
candidates.score_reasoning: Large national registry-based RCT providing clinically actionable lifetime revision risk data for TKA stratified by patient profile, directly applicable to preoperative counseling.
bullets: In robotic-assisted TKA, CR implants produced more balanced flexion-extension gaps than PS implants, while PS implants required less posterior femoral bone resection.
At two years, clinical outcomes were equivalent between CR and PS designs regardless of which implant was used.
For patients with varus deformity and an intact PCL, CR implants remain a reliable choice, while PS implants are preferred when flexion gap imbalance or PCL deficiency is present.

candidates.title: Operative Strategies for Treating Tibial Plateau Fractures in Patients Aged 55 Years and Older: A Five-Year Comparison of Acute Total Knee Arthroplasty with Open Reduction and Internal Fixation, Conversion Total Knee Arthroplasty, and Total Knee Arthroplasty for Osteoarthritis.
candidates.authors_short: Wahid M, Bellamy J, et al.
candidates.abstract: OBJECTIVES: To compare outcomes of acute total knee arthroplasty (TKA) for tibial plateau fracture in patients aged 55 years and older with matched patients undergoing open reduction and internal fixation (ORIF), conversion TKA after failed ORIF, and primary TKA for osteoarthritis. METHODS: Design: Retrospective cohort study with propensity score matching. SETTING: Federated multi-institutional electronic health records database (TriNetX United States Collaborative Network). PATIENT SELECTION CRITERIA: Patients aged ≥55 years with tibial plateau fracture treated with acute TKA, ORIF, or conversion TKA after failed ORIF were identified. A separate cohort undergoing primary TKA for osteoarthritis without fracture history was identified as a non-traumatic comparator. The study period was restricted to January 1, 2005 through December 31, 2020 to ensure a minimum of five years of potential follow-up for all included patients. OUTCOME MEASURES AND COMPARISONS: The primary outcome was revision surgery at 5 years, defined as conversion to TKA after ORIF and as revision TKA after arthroplasty. Secondary outcomes were a composite "return to the operating room (OR)" outcome (selected major reoperations), periprosthetic joint infection (PJI), surgical site infection (SSI), aseptic loosening, manipulation under anesthesia (MUA), and periprosthetic fracture. Three 1:1 propensity score-matched comparisons were performed (acute TKA versus ORIF; acute versus conversion TKA; acute TKA versus primary TKA for osteoarthritis), with risk ratios (RR) and 95% confidence intervals (CI) calculated. Subgroup analyses were stratified by age (55-70 years; ≥70 years). RESULTS: After matching, 1,321 patients per cohort were compared in the primary acute TKA versus ORIF analysis. Mean age was 66.1 years in the acute TKA cohort and 66.6 years in the ORIF cohort (range, 55 to 90 in both), and 65.3% and 66.7%, respectively, were female. Acute TKA had higher 5-year revision rates than ORIF (7.0% versus 0.8%; RR 8.36, 95% CI 4.50-15.56; P < 0.001) and elevated PJI rates (6.2% versus 1.3%; RR 4.82, 95% CI 2.88-8.09; P < 0.001). Return to OR rates did not differ significantly between acute TKA and ORIF (25.6% versus 23.5%; RR 1.09, 95% CI 0.95-1.25; P = 0.21). Revision did not differ between acute and conversion TKA (9.0% versus 10.0%; RR 0.89, 95% CI 0.58-1.35; P = 0.589) but was higher after acute TKA than after primary TKA for osteoarthritis (7.4% versus 3.5%; RR 2.12, 95% CI 1.48-3.00; P < 0.001). Revision was higher after acute TKA than ORIF in patients aged 55-70 years (9.3% versus 1.7%; RR 5.41, 95% CI 2.80-10.48; P < 0.001) and was not reportable in those aged ≥70 years owing to small cell counts. CONCLUSIONS: In patients aged 55 years and older, acute TKA for tibial plateau fracture was associated with higher risks of revision and complications compared with ORIF. Revision and complication rates after acute TKA were comparable with those after conversion TKA following failed ORIF but higher than those after primary TKA for osteoarthritis. Acute TKA should be reserved for patients at highest risk of ORIF failure requiring subsequent conversion to TKA. LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Level III, therapeutic study.
candidates.score_reasoning: Large retrospective propensity-matched database study comparing acute TKA vs ORIF for tibial plateau fractures in older patients, addressing a clinically important and evolving management question.
bullets: In patients 55 and older with tibial plateau fractures, acute TKA had a five-year revision rate of 7% and PJI rate of 6.2%, both significantly higher than ORIF at 0.8% and 1.3% respectively.
Revision rates after acute TKA were similar to those after conversion TKA following failed ORIF, meaning upfront TKA does not spare patients from the complication burden of a staged approach.
Acute TKA for tibial plateau fracture should be reserved for patients at high risk of ORIF failure, as ORIF remains the lower-risk option for most patients in this age group.

candidates.title: Antibiotic Nails Outperform Implant Retention in Preventing Recurrent Infections After Intramedullary Nail Fixation of Tibial Shaft Fractures Complicated by Infection.
candidates.authors_short: Wilhelm ZC, Kommu K, et al.
candidates.abstract: OBJECTIVES: To compare infection recurrence rates between patients treated with antibiotic nail versus implant retention for open tibial shaft fractures initially treated with an intramedullary (IM) nail complicated by infection. METHODS: Design: Retrospective cohort study. SETTING: Level I trauma center. PATIENT SELECTION CRITERIA: Adults with tibial shaft fractures (OTA/AO 42A-C) treated with an IM nail between 2007 and 2023 who developed deep surgical site infections after index fixation were included. OUTCOME MEASURES AND COMPARISONS: The primary outcome was infection recurrence within 2 years requiring reoperation and antibiotics. Secondary outcomes included amputation rate, all-cause mortality rate, days in hospital within 1 year of index infection surgery, time to recurrence, and number of surgeries needed after recurrence. The association between treatment and the study outcomes was estimated using Cox proportional hazards models, controlling for potential confounders. RESULTS: A total of 96 patients were included, 75 (78%) [62 males; median age 47 years (interquartile range (IQR), 31 to 53)] were treated with conversion to antibiotic nail and 21 (22%) [18 males; median age 36 years (IQR, 27 to 48)] with implant retention. The antibiotic nail group was more likely to have chronic infections, requiring surgery 6 or more weeks after index IM nail fixation (65% vs. 38%, P = 0.03). The 2-year infection recurrence rate was significantly lower with implant removal and antibiotic nail (33%) than with implant retention (54%) (HR, 0.43; 95% CI, 0.20 to 0.92; P = 0.03). For the secondary outcomes collected, only the average number of surgeries required after recurrence differed significantly between the two groups, with 3.9 for antibiotic nail and 3.0 for implant retention (IRR, 1.39; 95% CI, 1.01 to 1.91; P = 0.04). CONCLUSIONS: Conversion to an antibiotic nail was associated with lower rates of infection recurrence compared with implant retention. The overall infection recurrence rates of 33% in the antibiotic nail cohort and 54% in the implant retention cohort highlight the challenges associated with treating infection after IM nail fixation of tibial shaft fractures, regardless of treatment strategy. LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Therapeutic, Level III.
candidates.score_reasoning: Secondary analysis of two prospective RCTs examining timing of flap coverage in open fractures provides high-quality Level 2 evidence on infection risk thresholds directly applicable to trauma practice.
bullets: In infected tibial IM nails, converting to an antibiotic nail cut 2-year infection recurrence from 54% to 33% compared with keeping the original implant.
This applies to adults with deep infections after tibial shaft IM nailing, including those with chronic infections presenting more than 6 weeks out.
Antibiotic nail conversion is the preferred strategy for infection control, though one in three patients will still have recurrence and should be counseled accordingly.

candidates.title: Tranexamic Acid Administration is Associated With Lower Transfusion Rates and Wound Complications Following Revision Total Knee Arthroplasty for Periprosthetic Joint Infection.
candidates.authors_short: Kumaran P, Wier J, et al.
candidates.abstract: BACKGROUND: Tranexamic acid (TXA) is widely used in total joint arthroplasty, but data on its efficacy in periprosthetic joint infection (PJI) of the knee are scarce. We assessed TXA efficacy in revision total knee arthroplasty (TKA) for PJI. METHODS: A national database was queried for patients ≥18 years undergoing stage-one revision TKA for PJI from 2016 to 2023. Patients with and without TXA exposure were propensity matched. Multivariable logistic regression assessed primary outcomes (postoperative transfusion, bleeding complications, and wound complications) and secondary outcomes (thromboembolic complications). RESULTS: Overall, 13,247 TXA patients were matched 1:1 to 13,247 non-TXA patients on comorbidities, Charlson Comorbidity Index, demographics, hospital characteristics, and preoperative transfusion rates, all with standardized mean differences <0.10. Mean age was 67.4 years in both cohorts, with similar use of venous thromboembolic chemoprophylaxis. TXA was associated with decreased adjusted odds of postoperative transfusion (adjusted odds ratio [aOR]: 0.77, 95% confidence interval [CI]: 0.69-0.85, P < .001) and aggregate wound complications (aOR: 0.65, 95% CI: 0.60-0.70, P < .001), with similar odds of aggregate bleeding complications (aOR: 1.02, 95% CI: 0.95-1.09, P = .563). Odds of aggregate venous thromboembolism (aOR: 0.97, 95% CI: 0.82-1.13, P = .874), deep vein thrombosis (aOR: 1.00, 95% CI: 1.00-1.01, P = .309), and pulmonary embolism (aOR: 1.06, 95% CI: 0.83-1.34, P = .639) were similar. CONCLUSIONS: TXA was associated with lower rates of transfusion and aggregate wound complications, without increased venous thromboembolism risk, during revision TKA for PJI.
candidates.score_reasoning: Large matched database study (13,247 pairs) demonstrating TXA reduces transfusion and wound complications in revision TKA for PJI provides directly applicable perioperative management data.
bullets: TXA use during stage-one revision TKA for PJI reduced transfusion rates and wound complications without increasing clot risk.
These findings apply to patients averaging 67 years old undergoing revision knee arthroplasty specifically for periprosthetic joint infection.
Surgeons should consider routine TXA use in PJI revision cases, as the bleeding and infection context does not appear to negate its benefit or add thrombotic harm.

candidates.title: Local Bone Density of Preoperative CT: A Predictor of Clinically Significant Shortening and Varus Collapse of Well-Reduced Geriatric Intertrochanteric Hip Fractures.
candidates.authors_short: Kashyap J, Kuhn MZ, et al.
candidates.journal: The Journal of the American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons
candidates.abstract: INTRODUCTION: Intertrochanteric (IT) fractures are the most common geriatric hip fracture, with early fixation failure contributing to high morbidity and mortality. Lower bone density, as measured by Hounsfield units (HU) from CT scans, is predictive of various long bone fractures and fracture fixation failure, although its role in IT fractures is less well described. We aimed to assess the association between local bone density and radiographic outcomes after cephalomedullary nail (CMN) fixation of well-reduced geriatric IT fractures, hypothesizing that lower HU measurements are associated with increased rates of clinically significant shortening and varus collapse. METHODS: We retrospectively reviewed patients older than 60 years with low-energy IT fractures treated with a long or short CMN between 2017 and 2024 at a single institution. Fractures with varus malreduction or tip apex distance >25 mm were excluded. Radiographs were assessed postoperatively and at 6 to 24-week follow-up to evaluate for shortening and change in the neck-shaft angle. Hounsfield unit measurements of the proximal femur were obtained from injury CT scans. Two-sample t-tests, simple linear regression, and multivariate logistic regression were used to analyze the relationship between HU and shortening/varus collapse. RESULTS: Among 103 patients (74 women, 29 men; mean age 79.3 ± 9.8 years), the mean local bone density was 193.3 ± 63.4 HU. Patients with clinically significant shortening or varus collapse (n = 38) had significantly lower HU than those without (n = 65) (160.9 vs. 212.3 HU, P < 0.0001). HU was independently associated with shortening/varus collapse (OR 0.98, P < 0.01) and negatively correlated with magnitude of shortening (R2 = 0.091, P < 0.01). An exploratory threshold of 150 HU significantly predicted shortening. CONCLUSIONS: Lower local bone density predicts shortening/varus collapse after CMN fixation of well-reduced geriatric IT fractures, despite optimization of modifiable surgical factors. An exploratory threshold of 150 HU may identify patients at risk of shortening within 24 weeks postoperatively.
candidates.score_reasoning: Local CT-based Hounsfield unit measurements predicting fixation failure in intertrochanteric fractures offers a novel, practical preoperative risk stratification tool for hip fracture surgeons.
bullets: In geriatric intertrochanteric fractures fixed with a cephalomedullary nail, patients who developed shortening or varus collapse had meaningfully lower proximal femur bone density on CT than those who did not (161 vs. 212 Hounsfield units).
A local bone density threshold of 150 Hounsfield units on preoperative CT identifies patients at elevated risk for clinically significant collapse within 6 months, even after well-executed fixation.
For orthopaedic surgeons treating elderly hip fractures, routine CT Hounsfield unit measurement can flag high-risk patients before surgery and guide counseling about expected implant performance.

candidates.title: Safety and Clinical Impact of Emergency Department Closed Reduction for Gartland Type III Supracondylar Humerus Fractures.
candidates.authors_short: Kelley NH, Carroll CJ, et al.
candidates.abstract: BACKGROUND: Pediatric type 3 supracondylar humerus fractures (SCHFs) are typically immobilized in situ before definitive operative fixation because of concern for neurovascular injury during closed reduction. This study assesses the safety and clinical outcomes of emergency department (ED) closed reduction versus in situ splinting for type 3 SCHFs before definitive fixation. METHODS: A retrospective review was conducted of all pediatric extension-type 3 SCHFs that underwent closed reduction versus no reduction by orthopaedic surgery residents in the ED at a single Level 1 trauma center over a 5-year period. Data included pre- and postreduction neurovascular examinations, multiple radiographic parameters, durations of time between injury, consult, and reduction to the operating room (OR), total operative time, and OR fluoroscopy duration. RESULTS: Of 112 patients, 54 underwent closed reduction (CR) while 58 were not reduced (NR). Nine (20%) patients in the CR group and 9 (18%) patients in the NR group had abnormal neurological exams on presentation. Four (8%) patients in the CR group and 2 (4%) patients in the NR group had abnormal vascular exams. All 4 patients who underwent closed reduction had improved vascular exams from Doppler-able to palpable radial pulses (P=0.12). No vascular injuries occurred with closed reduction. Importantly, 6 patients in the NR group with initial normal exams developed abnormal neurological deficits while awaiting surgical fixation (P=0.03). The CR group demonstrated significantly improved radiographic parameters postreduction, including AP and lateral displacement, anterior humeral line displacement, lateral Baumann angle, and hourglass angle. The time from consult or reduction to OR was significantly less for the NR group compared with the CR group (9.83 vs. 13.45 h; P<0.01). The time from injury to the OR was also significantly less in the NR group (21.0 vs. 17.0 h; P=0.02). The CR group trended towards shorter operative times (33 vs. 40 min; P=0.15). CONCLUSION: Closed reduction of pediatric type 3 SCHFs in the ED by orthopaedic surgery residents is safe and can improve both neurovascular deficits and radiographic fracture alignment. As most pediatric extremity fractures undergo closed reduction in the ED, type 3 SCHFs should not be considered an exception. LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Level III-retrospective comparative study.
candidates.score_reasoning: Large population-based cohort study from Finland (2778 patients) examining osteoporosis medication effects on hip arthroplasty outcomes after femoral neck fracture is relevant to fragility fracture management.
bullets: Emergency department closed reduction of Gartland III supracondylar fractures by orthopaedic residents caused no vascular injuries and improved pulseless limbs from Doppler-detectable to palpable radial pulses.
Six children in the splinted-in-situ group developed new neurological deficits while waiting for the operating room, compared to none in the closed reduction group.
For pediatric Gartland III supracondylar fractures, ED closed reduction is safe and should be performed routinely rather than leaving the fracture unreduced until surgery.

candidates.title: Is There an Association Between Abnormal Patellofemoral Morphology and Patellofemoral Osteochondritis Dissecans in Pediatric Patients?
candidates.authors_short: Kuka CC, Syed AN, et al.
candidates.journal: The American journal of sports medicine
candidates.abstract: BACKGROUND: The cause of patellofemoral osteochondritis dissecans (OCD) lesions is not clear. Biomechanical factors, such as abnormal patellofemoral morphology seen in patients with patellofemoral instability (PFI), may contribute to the development of patellofemoral OCD. PURPOSE: To determine whether anatomic risk factors associated with PFI are also present in patients with patellofemoral OCD. STUDY DESIGN: Case-control study; Level of evidence, 3. METHODS: The authors compared 3 groups of pediatric (≤ 19 years of age) patients evaluated at the study institution from 2001 to 2024: (1) those with patellofemoral OCD and no history of PFI, (2) those with recurrent (≥2 dislocations) PFI with no evidence of OCD, and (3) those without known knee pathology (controls). Patients were propensity score matched 1:1:1 by age, sex, and body mass index. Measurements of patellar height, position, translocation, and trochlear dysplasia were collected from magnetic resonance imaging scans obtained before any intervention and compared between patients with patellofemoral OCD and PFI, and patients with patellofemoral OCD and controls. Statistical analysis was performed in R Version 4.3.2. RESULTS: In total, 306 patients (102 in each group) met inclusion criteria. Caton-Deschamps index (CDI) and tibial tuberosity-trochlear groove (TT-TG) distance were significantly higher in patients with OCD compared to controls (CDI: 1.0 ± 0.16 for controls vs 1.1 ± 0.17 for OCD, P < .001; TT-TG: 12.9 ± 4.0 for controls vs 14.6 ± 4.1 for OCD, P = .004). All other measures of patellar and trochlear dysplasia were not significantly different between controls and patients with OCD. All measures of patellar and trochlear morphology differed significantly between OCD and PFI groups, and control and PFI groups. Logistic regression analysis indicated increased risk of patellofemoral OCD in patients with an increase in CDI (OR, 1.47; P < .001) and TT-TG (OR, 1.23; P < .001). CONCLUSION: Morphological characteristics of PFI do not appear to be associated with patellofemoral OCD. Rather, patients with patellofemoral OCD have knee anatomy that appears to be distinct from both patients with recurrent instability and controls with normal knee anatomy.
candidates.score_reasoning: Case-control study of patellofemoral OCD and morphological risk factors in 306 propensity-matched pediatric patients provides novel anatomic insights into an uncommon but clinically challenging condition.
bullets: Pediatric patients with patellofemoral OCD have mildly elevated patellar height and TT-TG distance compared to normal controls, but their anatomy does not resemble the more pronounced dysplasia seen in recurrent patellar instability.

Patellofemoral OCD appears to occupy its own anatomic category, distinct from both normal knees and knees with instability, suggesting a unique biomechanical environment contributes to lesion development.

In skeletally immature patients presenting with patellofemoral OCD, surgeons should not assume underlying instability anatomy, as standard instability risk factors are largely absent in this population.
